# Lab overview

Plastic pollution is a major and growing problem, negatively affecting oceans and wildlife health. [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/plastic-pollution) publishes plastic-waste data globally, by country, and over time. This lab focuses on country-level data from **2010**.

National Geographic also ran a data-visualization communication contest on plastic waste, which you can browse [here](https://www.nationalgeographic.org/funding-opportunities/innovation-challenges/plastic/dataviz/).

```{marginfigure}
You already practiced the GitHub + RStudio Cloud workflow in Lab 01. The steps below are a short review.
```

## Learning goals

By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

A. Visualize numerical and categorical data with histograms, density plots, box plots, violin plots, and scatterplots.
B. Choose plot types and `ggplot2` settings (faceting, transparency, color) that make comparisons readable.
C. Interpret the shape, center, spread, outliers, and associations you see in a plot.
D. Recreate a visualization from a description and a target figure.
E. Keep building fluency with R, RStudio, Git, and GitHub.

## Deliverable

Complete **`lab-02-starter.Rmd`**. Your finished starter file should contain your code, plots, and written responses and should Knit successfully from top to bottom.

**The instructions file tells you what to do; the starter file is where your assignment work belongs, except for completing the honor-code signature above.**

## Reproducibility rule

Throughout EAES 380, your analysis should work **from top to bottom**. Code that works only because you previously ran something in the Console is not reproducible.

**Knit frequently.** Knitting is one of the best ways to discover whether your document actually contains everything needed to reproduce your work.

## Before asking for help

First check:

- Did you run the relevant chunks from top to bottom?
- Did you spell every object and variable name exactly as shown? R is case-sensitive.
- Are all parentheses, quotation marks, and backticks closed?
- Did you load the packages needed by your code?
- Does the error message point to a particular chunk or line?
- Have you tried Knitting the document to identify where the problem first occurs?

If you still cannot resolve the problem, ask your instructor or TA and show them the code and error message.

# Packages and data

## Load packages

We will use the **tidyverse** package for this analysis. The package is already **installed**, but you must still **load** it into each new R session.

Navigate to `lab-02-starter.Rmd` and run the `load-packages` chunk.

```{r load-packages-demo, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
library(tidyverse)
```

## Load the data

The dataset lives in the `data` folder of your repository. Read it in with the `load-data` chunk in your starter file (or run the code below in the Console while you explore).

```{r load-data-demo, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
plastic_waste <- read_csv("data/plastic-waste.csv")
```

```{marginfigure}
**Hint:** "Per capita" means "per person."
```

Variable descriptions:

- `code`: 3-letter country code
- `entity`: Country name
- `continent`: Continent name
- `year`: Year
- `gdp_per_cap`: GDP per capita, constant 2011 international dollars
- `plastic_waste_per_cap`: Plastic waste per capita in kg/person
- `mismanaged_plastic_waste_per_cap`: Mismanaged plastic waste per capita in kg/person
- `mismanaged_plastic_waste`: Tonnes of mismanaged plastic waste
- `coastal_pop`: Number of people living on or near the coast
- `total_pop`: Total population according to Gapminder

A few countries that span Europe and Asia appear twice in the table, once under each continent. That is a feature of how this file was compiled, not an error in your code.

# Exercises

For each exercise:

A. Read the prompt here.
B. Complete the corresponding section in `lab-02-starter.Rmd`.
C. Run your code and inspect the output.
D. Write any requested interpretation in complete sentences.
E. Knit before moving on when a checkpoint is indicated.

**Note:** Code chunk labels are already provided for all eight exercises (for example, `{r plastic-waste-continent}`). If you add any new chunks of your own, give them a label too.

Let's start by looking at the distribution of plastic waste per capita in 2010 using `geom_histogram()`.

```{r plastic_waste_per_cap-hist, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(data = plastic_waste, aes(x = plastic_waste_per_cap)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2)
```

```{marginfigure}
`ggplot2` drops missing values from the plotted variable and may print a warning. That is expected here: many countries do not have a recorded plastic-waste value.
```

One country stands out as an unusual observation at the high end of the distribution.

One way to identify that country is to filter the data for countries where plastic waste per capita is **greater than 3.5 kg/person**.

```{r plastic_waste_per_cap-max, eval=TRUE}
plastic_waste %>%
  filter(plastic_waste_per_cap > 3.5)
```

Did you expect this result?

You might look up Trinidad and Tobago to see why plastic waste per capita is so high there, or whether this value is a data error. Either way, keep this country in mind: it will pull the scale of several later plots.

## Exercise 1 — Faceted histograms by continent

**Goal:** Compare the distribution of a numerical variable across levels of a categorical variable.

Plot, using **histograms**, the distribution of plastic waste per capita **faceted by continent**.

- What can you say about how the continents compare to each other in terms of plastic waste per capita?

A useful starting point is the histogram above plus `facet_wrap(~ continent)`. You may reuse `binwidth = 0.2` or choose a bin width that makes the comparison readable.

### Exercise 1 checkpoint

🧶 ✅ ⬆️ **Knit, commit, and push.** Suggested commit message: `Complete Exercise 1`.

--

**NOTE:** From this point onward, the plots and printed output are not displayed in these instructions. Run the demonstration chunks in this file or type them into your starter file so that you can see the output yourself.

Then, for each exercise, write the required code in `lab-02-starter.Rmd` and interpret what you see.

Another way of visualizing numerical data is a **density plot**.

```{r plastic_waste_per_cap-dens}
ggplot(data = plastic_waste, aes(x = plastic_waste_per_cap)) +
  geom_density()
```

We can also compare density distributions across continents by mapping continent to the color of the curves.

```{r plastic_waste_per_cap-dens-color}
ggplot(data = plastic_waste, 
       mapping = aes(x = plastic_waste_per_cap, 
                     color = continent)) +
  geom_density()
```

The resulting plot may be a little difficult to read, so let's also fill the curves.

```{r plastic_waste_per_cap-dens-color-fill}
ggplot(data = plastic_waste, 
       mapping = aes(x = plastic_waste_per_cap, 
                     color = continent, 
                     fill = continent)) +
  geom_density()
```

Hmm, still not ideal.

Overlapping fills make it difficult to see the continents that were plotted first, because later layers sit on top of them.

We can change the transparency of the fill with the `alpha` argument. `alpha` takes values between 0 and 1: 0 is completely transparent and 1 is completely opaque.

There is no single "correct" value. Try a few.

```{r plastic_waste_per_cap-dens-color-fill-alpha}
ggplot(data = plastic_waste, 
       mapping = aes(x = plastic_waste_per_cap, 
                     color = continent, 
                     fill = continent)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7)
```

This still does not look great...

## Exercise 2 — Density plots with a better alpha

**Goal:** Use transparency so that overlapping distributions remain visible.

Recreate the filled density plots above using a **lower** alpha level that works better for displaying the density curves for all continents.

## Exercise 3 — Mapped aesthetics vs. geom arguments

**Goal:** Distinguish variables that are mapped from data and settings that are fixed by you.

In 1–2 complete sentences, explain why we defined the `color` and `fill` of the curves by **mapping aesthetics** of the plot, but we defined the `alpha` level as an argument of the plotting geom.

Another way to compare a numerical variable across groups is with side-by-side **box plots**.

```{r plastic_waste_per_cap-box}
ggplot(data = plastic_waste, 
       mapping = aes(x = continent, 
                     y = plastic_waste_per_cap)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

## Exercise 4 — Violin plots

**Goal:** Compare what box plots and violin plots each make visible.

Convert the side-by-side box plots from the previous chunk to [violin plots](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_violin.html).

Then answer both questions in complete sentences:

- What do the violin plots reveal that the box plots do not?
- What features are apparent in the box plots but not in the violin plots?

**Goal:** Compare the strength of two associations using separate scatterplots.

The word "smooth" should help you [pick which geom to use](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/index.html#section-geoms).

## Exercise 8 — Recreate and interpret a plot

**Goal:** Rebuild a complete `ggplot2` figure from a target plot and interpret it in context.

Recreate the following plot in your starter file (copying and pasting the code is fine) and interpret what you see in the context of the data.

```{r recreate-viz-demo, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
plastic_waste %>% 
  mutate(coastal_pop_prop = coastal_pop / total_pop) %>%
  filter(plastic_waste_per_cap < 3) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = coastal_pop_prop, y = plastic_waste_per_cap, color = continent)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(color = "black") +
    scale_color_viridis_d() +
    labs(x = "Coastal population proportion (coastal / total population)", 
         y = "Plastic waste per capita", 
         color = "Continent",
         title = "Plastic waste vs. coastal population proportion",
         subtitle = "by continent") +
    theme_minimal()
```

Your written interpretation should address the overall pattern, what the smooth curve is doing, and what the plot suggests about countries with a large share of people living on the coast. Two to four complete sentences is enough.
